title: "LoRA"
description: "A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that learns low-rank weight updates while keeping pretrained weights fixed."
term: "LoRA"
letter: "L"
category: "LLM Engineering"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

LoRA lets an engineer adapt a large pretrained model without training every
parameter. It freezes the original weights and learns a much smaller update
that can be added to selected layers.

## Technical explanation

For a pretrained weight matrix $W_0$, LoRA represents a trainable update as a
product of two lower-rank matrices:

$$
W = W_0 + \Delta W,\qquad \Delta W = BA
$$

where $A$ and $B$ have a chosen small rank $r$. Implementations commonly scale
the update by a factor such as $\alpha/r$. The pretrained matrix is frozen,
while the smaller matrices are optimized on the adaptation data.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

LoRA can reduce the trainable parameter count, optimizer state, and storage
needed for task-specific adaptations. Teams can keep a shared base model and
manage multiple smaller adapters, while still evaluating quality, latency,
and memory for their deployment setup.

## How it works

LoRA inserts trainable low-rank matrices into selected layers, often
attention projections. During fine-tuning, gradients update those matrices
rather than the frozen base weights. Depending on the framework and serving
design, the adapter can remain separate or be merged into the base weights
for inference.

## Practical example

A team adapts a pretrained language model to follow a domain-specific writing
style. It trains and stores a small LoRA adapter rather than maintaining a
fully fine-tuned copy of all base-model parameters.

## Common misconceptions

- LoRA is a fine-tuning technique, not a new base-model architecture.
- Low-rank updates reduce trainable parameters but do not guarantee lower inference latency in every serving setup.
- A small adapter still needs representative data and careful evaluation.
